Q. How do you diagnose AML?

 

●      Percentage → >/= 20%[QZ1]  immature appearing mononuclear cells in the peripheral blood, aspirate or core biopsy

○      Or CG abnormality not requiring 20% blasts (t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17)

●      Myeloid lineage → diagnosed by demonstrating a myeloid immunophenotype.

●      A myeloid immunophenotype is essentially defined as anything that isn’t T-cell, B-cell, acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage, or blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm

 

Q. What are the criteria for “acute undifferentiated leukemia”?

●      1) Blasts express no more than one membrane marker for any given lineage

●      2) By definition → lack lineage ANY defining markers outlined in MPAL classification (ie. cCD3, CD19, cMPO etc.).

●      As well, they must lack specific cytologic features such as megakaryoblasts or plasmacytoid dendritic cells.

●      An extensive immunophenotyping panel should be performed → to evaluate the possibility of uncommon or ambiguous leukemias (NK-cell precursors, plasmacytoid dendritic cell, basophils, etc) or non-hematopoietic malignancies

●      Cannot have any of the recurrent CG abnormalities

-        Favorable

-        Intermediate (I/II)

-        Unfavorable

 

Q. What is a favorable risk profile for AML based on molecular studies and cytogenetics?

 

●      1) Core binding factors leukemias

○      t(8;21) RUNX1-RUN1T1

○      Inv(16)/t(16;16) CBFB-MYH11

●      2) APL with PML-RARA, t(15;17)

●      3) Mutated NPM1 without FLT3 ITD (normal karyotype)

●      4) Biallelic mutated CEBPA (normal karyotype)

Q. What is an intermediate risk profile for AML based on molecular studies and cytogenetics (3)? (Note 2017 ELN as above got rid of Int-1 and Int-2)

●      Mutated NPM1 and FLT3-ITD hi

●      Wild-type NPM1 and FLT3-ITD low

●      Wild-type NPM1 without FLT3-ITD = NORMAL.

●      All above with normal karyotype

●      t(9;11) MLLT3-KMT2A

●      Cytogenetics abnormalities not classified as favorable or adverse

Q. What is an adverse risk profile for AML based on molecular studies and cytogenetics (4)?

●      Inv(3)/t(3;3) GATA2-MECOM

●      t(6;9) DEK-NUP214

●      KMT2A (MLL) translocations

●      Ph+ t(9:22)

●      -5 of del(5q), -7, abnl (17p)

●      Complex karyotype

●      Monosomal karyotype

●      ALSO - NPM1(WT) with HIGH FLT3 allele burden. This is BAD. Also in ELN revision

●      Mut RUNX1, mut ASXL1, mut TP53

FLOW CYTOMETRY PRINCIPLES

ALOT: acute leukemia orientation tube - First a screening panel including lineage markers and immature markers (CD34/TdT, HLA-DR) allows the classification of most cases into the broad categories of myeloid (MPO positive), B-cell (CD19, CD79a, cCD22) or T-cell (cCD3) and, less frequently, mixed phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL).

AML with recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities

Recurring cytogenetic abnormalities

Specific balanced translocations and mutations

There are 8 categories related to specific balanced cytogenetic abnormalities included in the category of AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities, including 1 provisional entity. Of those, acute promyelocytic leukemia with, AML with t(8;21)(q22;q22.1); RUNX1-RUNX1T1 and AML with inv(16)(p13.1q22) or t(16;16)(p13.1;q22); CBFB-MYH11 may be diagnosed as acute leukemia in the correct clinical setting even if blast cells are less than 20% in the blood and bone marrow. All of the full entities of AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities “trump” other categories with the exception of therapy-related myeloid neoplasms. These same balanced translocations may certainly occur after cytotoxic therapy and should be noted due to their prognostic significance, but they should be considered as therapy-related. Olney et al demonstrated that balanced translocations historically associated with a favorable prognosis in de novo AML, also tend to have an improved prognosis in the therapy-related setting when compared to therapy-related disease overall [11] . The prognosis of the therapy-related group was less favorable, however, when compared to de novo AML cases with the same balanced translocation. For this reason, the clinical advisory committee recommended that such cases have a primary designation of therapy-related myeloid neoplasm with a notation of the cytogenetic abnormality rather than placing such cases directly in the AML with recurrent genetic abnormality group.

The 2016 WHO Classification contains 2 full entities related to specific gene mutations, AML with mutated NPM1 and AML with biallelic mutations of CEBPA. Similar to the specific balanced translocations in the category of AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities, these mutations are usually early events that are disease defining. They are uncommon after cytotoxic therapy, but such a history would take precedent over the mutation. Rarely, myeloid neoplasms such as myelodysplastic syndromes and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia acquire NPM1 mutations at a later stage of the disease, often associated with acute leukemia transformation [1213] , and such cases would not fall into the AML with mutated NPM1 category and should be diagnosed as AML with myelodysplasia-related changes due to the prior disease.

AML with t(8;21) → now AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion

Q. What are the key morphological features of AML with t(8;21) (RUNX1-RUNX1T1)?

●      M2 morphology

●      Prominent neutrophil maturation may be present.

●      Blasts reported as large with abundant basophilic cytoplasm often containing numerous azurophilic granules (occasionally large and chunky pseudo Chediak Higashi granules) and perinuclear clearing (hofs)

●      ABNORMAL NEUTROPHILS AND PRECURSORS: SALMON-COLORED GRANULES AND DYSPLASTIC NUCLEAR, CYTOPLASMIC VACUOLES

●      Long slender Auer rods

●      Increased eosinophil precursors without cytological abnormalities

●      Blasts are large, with a background of myeloid maturation, resemble M2 AML

●      CD34+, variable CD13 CD33; aberrant expression of CD19w, many express CD56, PAX5 frequently expressed when cases are studies by IHC, CD79a may be expressed

Blast (black solid arrow) and background of maturing myeloid elements in AML with t(8;21) show atypical granulation, including a Chediak-Higashi-like granule (black curved arrow) and salmon-colored granules (black open arrow), which is a relatively unique feature of this entity. Immunophenotypic features of AML with t(8; 21), bone marrow aspirate. Side scatter (SS) is plotted against antigen expression. Red, neutrophils; green, monocytes (confirmed as such by expression of CD14 and CD36 [data not shown] as they could otherwise have been interpreted as degranulated neutrophils); cyan, blast cells; magenta, lymphocytes. There are two distinct populations of monocytes and blast cells, although almost with a continuum. The blast cells express CD34 and weak CD33, as well as CD13 and CD117, but not CD11b (which stains monocytes and neutrophils). Blast cells, monocytes, and part of the neutrophil population express CD56. There is aberrant expression of CD19 by the blast cells. (Bain, B. J. and M. C. Bene (2019). "Morphological and Immunophenotypic Clues to the WHO Categories of Acute Myeloid Leukaemia." Acta Haematol 141(4): 232-244.)

AML with inv(16)/t(16;16) → now AML with CBFB::MYH11 fusion

Q. What are the key morphological features of AML with inv(16)/t(16;16) (CBFB-MYH11)?

●      Often myelomonocytic features with abnormal eosinophils that have larger, purple-violet granules (harlequin cells)

●      AML M4EO

●      The peripheral blood features of this category of CBF AML are not distinctive. Usually, the characteristics are those of acute myelomonocytic leukaemia, but there is variation from case to case. There is sometimes eosinophilia with the mature eosinophils showing little cytological abnormality. The bone marrow morphology is more distinctive, usually with an increase in eosinophils and their precursors, the latter showing large proeosinophilic granules, which have basophilic staining characteristics (Fig. 9). Abnormal eosinophil precursors are almost always present, even when the number of eosinophils is low. The diagnosis can often but not always be suspected from the cytological features.

●      The immunophenotype is that of myeloid blasts, with frequent expression of monocytic markers such as CD4, CD36, or CD38 among those most often tested [10, 11]. Part of the blastic population may express neutrophil markers such as CD15 and/or CD65. The neutrophilic/ monocytic differentiation trend of these blasts also translates into clear expression of CD11b, an antigen that is generally more strongly expressed by monocytes than by neutrophils. CD2 is often positive. Assessment of the cytological (particularly in the bone marrow) and immunophenotypic features suggests this diagnosis in the majority of cases, before FISH and/or conventional cytogenetic analysis disclose the inversion or translocation.

 

Harlequin cells. Eosinophils with large purple-violet granules resembling basophilic granules. Dysplastic eosinophils with metachromatic granules are often referred to as harlequin cells.

 

AML with t(9;11) → now AML with KMT2A rearrangement

Q. What are the key morphological features of AML with t(9;11) KMT2A-MLLT3?

●      No specific morphologic findings but is usually associated with monocytic features.

●      May present as myeloid sarcoma

●      Cytological features are usually those of acute monoblastic leukaemia but sometimes of acute monocytic or acute myelomonocytic leukaemia. There are no specific cytological clues to this diagnosis.

●      The immunophenotype shows the presence of monocytic markers, without expression of CD19. Some cases are CD4 positive. There may be some asynchrony in the expression of CD33 (positive) and CD13 (negative), and CD34 is often lacking. Monocytic differentiation may also be deduced from some co-expression (often weak) of CD15 and/or CD65, usually in the absence of CD14 [4]. There are no strong morphological or immunophenotypic clues to this diagnosis.

AML with t(6;9) → now AML with DEK::NUP214 fusion

Q. What are the key morphological features of AML with t(6;9) DEK-NUP214?

●      Commonly associated with multilineage dysplasia and basophilia.

●      This category of AML sometimes presents as AML with maturation and sometimes as acute myelomonocytic leukaemia. There are often dysplastic features. Sometimes there is basophilic differentiation, and in these cases the cytogenetic diagnosis may be suspected (Fig. 10). Both peripheral blood and bone marrow basophils can be increased. Some patients also have an increase in bone marrow eosinophils.

●      The immunophenotype of AML carrying this anomaly has been reported by Oyarzo et al. [12] as that of immature myeloid progenitors co-expressing in most cases CD34, CD117, CD33, and CD13 together with CD9 and CD38. In a previous smaller series, Alsabeh et al. [13] reported a more variable expression of CD34. This diagnosis may be suspected in cases with increased basophils but otherwise there are no strong morphological or immunophenotypic indicators.

●     

AML with t(3;3)/inv(3) → now AML with MECOM rearrangement

Q. What are the key morphological features of AML with t(3;3)/inv(3) GATA2-MECOM?

●      Marked thrombocytosis occurs in 7-22% of cases.

●      Multilineage dysplasia is common with often increased and dysplastic small and non-lobated megakaryocytes present.

●      This category of AML often has dysplastic megakaryocytes (Fig. 11) and, unusually among cases of AML, can have a normal or even an increased platelet count. Differentiation can be granulocytic, myelomonocytic, or monoblastic/monocytic, but megakaryocytic differentiation is over-represented. Trilineage myelodysplasia can be present.

●      The immunophenotype is that of immature myeloid cells co-expressing CD34, CD117, CD13, and CD33 with MPO often being negative [14, 15]. Expression of CD7, CD11c, CD11b, and CD123 is frequent, but positivity for CD56 is seen less often [14]. When megakaryocytic differentiation is present, it can be confirmed by CD41, CD42, and/or CD61 positivity. Monocytic forms may express CD14.

●      Only cases with a normal or increased platelet count and with dysplastic megakaryocytes are likely to be suspected on morphological and immunophenotypic grounds. Otherwise, making a distinction from AML with myelodysplasia-related changes is difficult.

●     

AML with t(1;22) → now AML with RBM15::MRTFA fusion

Q. What are the key morphological features of AML with t(1;22) RBM15-MKL1

●      The blasts are similar to those in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (subtype of AML, NOS).

●      This subtype of AML typically occurs in infants and this, combined with the cytological features (basophilic blast cells with cytoplasmic blebs), can lead to a strong suspicion of the diagnosis (Fig. 12). Immunophenotyping is useful in confirming the megakaryoblastic differentiation [16]. There are expressions of CD41, CD42, and/ or CD61. Search for expression of these antigens can be prompted by the morphology of the blast cells. If there is no connexion with a morphology platform, at least one of these specificities should be included in the immunophenotyping panel in all cases of AML in infants[9]. In the event of unexpected faint or absent surface labelling, a stronger signal can be obtained by investigation of intracytoplasmic expression of these megakaryocyte-associated markers. Consideration of the cytological and immunophenotypic features in the context of the age of the patient often leads to suspicion of this diagnosis.

●     

AML with BCR-ABL1 → AML with BCR::ABL1 fusion

Q. What is the Provisional entity: AML with BCR-ABL1 - what is the rationale for its inclusion - how are these cases defined?

●      Rarely, cases of apparent de novo AML with BCR-ABL1 have been reported.

●      Rationale → these cases are felt to warrant provisional category as potentially targetable genetic lesion is present (BCR-ABL1 fusion), though paucity of cases makes significance of this uncertain.

●      Definition → Based on 6 cases over 8 year period at MGH that → defined de novo cases as AML with t(9:22) on cytogenetics with NO evidence of chronic phase CML before diagnosis or after induction.

●      This is a provisional WHO category of AML. There are no specific cytological features.

●      Immunophenotyping shows expression of myeloid antigens with aberrant expression of CD7 and CD19 appearing to be common. However, in cases expressing CD19 it is important to exclude a diagnosis of mixed phenotype acute leukaemia [9]. Distinctive cytological or immunophenotypic features that would permit suspicion of this entity have not yet been identified.

AML with BCR-ABL1 is a new provisional entity in the WHO Classification and was added to recognize these rare de novo AML cases that may benefit from tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy. While most blast proliferations with a BCR-ABL1 fusion, usually caused by t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2), represent blast transformation of CML, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, or mixed phenotype acute leukemia, rare cases of de novo AML with BCR-ABL1 occur. This rare AML type represents less than 1% of all cases, with a possible male predominance 222324 . It is difficult to distinguish on an individual basis de novo AML with BCR-ABL1 from myeloid blast transformation of CML, and exclusion of an occult chronic phase of CML preceding the diagnosis of AML, or post-therapy for AML, is essential for diagnosis. Cases of de novo AML with BCR-ABL1 appear to differ from blast crisis of CML by having less frequent splenomegaly and basophilia and slightly lower marrow cellularity.

AML with NPM1 Mutation

This subtype of AML can have either: (i) the cytological features of acute myeloblastic leukaemia with or without maturation (with Auer rods sometimes being present) and with expression of MPO, or (ii) the cytological features of acute myelomonocytic or monocytic/monoblastic correlation between the cytological category and the immunophenotype. A distinctive feature that can be present is the presence of leukaemic blasts with cup-shaped nuclei. This is seen particularly in cases with coexisting FLT3-internal tandem duplication [18, 19] (Fig. 13). Immunophenotyping shows expression of CD33, CD117, and MPO in cases with myeloblastic differentiation. Cases with monocytic differentiation (Fig. 14) typically show expression of CD64, CD14, and/or CD11b. Overall, about two thirds of cases do not express CD34 and about one third do not express HLA-DR, yielding an “APL-like” immunophenotype [17]. In one large series, 32% of cases were negative for both CD34 and HLA-DR, these falling very largely into the group with myeloblastic differentiation; such cases were more likely to express CD56 and show weak or negative expression of CD13 [17]. The expression of CD4 or CD19 has also been re-ported in a series of AML patients with mutated NPM1 and normal karyotype [20].

It is possible to suspect this diagnosis on cytological and immunophenotypic grounds when cup-shaped nuclei are present with HLA-DR, CD34, or both being negative or, in the absence of the typical cytological features, when there is an immunophenotype resembling that of APL, CD34-negative, HLA-DR negative, but with the SSC expected of normal myeloid progenitors [21].

Arber, D: AML with mutated NPM1 is now a full entity, and as mentioned above, the presence of this gene mutation in a de novo case of AML takes precedence over a diagnosis of AML with myelodysplasia-related changes. Multilineage dysplasia is present in approximately 1-quarter of cases and does not appear to have prognostic importance in de novo cases. Additional mutation studies, especially FLT3 -ITD and possibly DNMT3A , are necessary, however, to determine the appropriate prognosis for this disease category [32] .


Caveats and Pearls

·       Cytoplasmic NPM1 positivity by IHC is a surrogate for NPM1 mutation

·       Acute monocytic and myelomonocytic leukemias often have NPM1 mutations

AML with Biallelic CEBPA Mutation → now AML with CEBPA mutation

There are no cytological clues to this diagnosis, although Mannelli et al. [22] reported a frequent association with erythroid dysplasia. The same authors performed an extensive immunophenotypic exploration of their cases, comparing them with wild-type CEBPA and monoallelic CEBPA mutation. They noted a high expression of antigens indicative of immaturity (CD34, CD117, and HLA-DR) together with strong MPO and asynchronous expression of antigens typical of more mature cells, CD15 and CD65. CD7 and CD56 were also frequently expressed. Interestingly, CD64 was found to be expressed not only by blasts, but also by neutrophils (unusual and mostly characteristic of activated neutrophils and of monocytes). The erythroid dysplasia detectable morphologically was reflected in flow cytometry with features of immature erythroblasts being observed, respectively CD117 and CD105 (endoglin) positivity associated with low levels of CD36 and CD71 [22]. By analysing SSC and the expression of six antigens on blast cells, neutrophils, monocytes, and erythroid cells, these authors were able to predict CEBPA biallelic mutation and thus target molecular analysis [22]. The cytological features are not distinctive but detailed immunophenotypic analysis can permit suspicion of this diagnosis.

·       The prior category of AML with mutated CEBPA has now been modified to require biallelic mutation of this gene, because only the biallelic mutation group is associated with an improved prognosis when compared to other AML types 33343536 . This revised category is now considered a full entity, and supersedes AML with myelodysplasia-related changes in de novo cases.



AML with RUNX1 Mutation → no longer exists

There are no cytological features suggestive of this anomaly although this genetic subtype is over-represented among cases of MPO-negative AML. In a large Taiwanese study, Tang et al. [23] found 4 out of 10 patients with French-American-British (FAB) M0 AML to have a RUNX1 mutation.

The same authors also reported that the blast cells usually expressed CD34, CD13, and HLA-DR, whereas expres-sion of CD33 and CD15 was less common than in other cases of AML (77 and 28%, respectively), suggesting immature cells; CD56 was also expressed less often, being seen in only 13% of cases. CD19 was not expressed in any case.

·       A provisional category of AML with mutated RUNX1 has been added to the classification for cases of de novo AML with this mutation that are not associated with MDS-related cytogenetic abnormalities. The incidence of this mutation is 4% to 16% in AML, but it is also associated with prior MDS, radiation exposure or chemotherapy; findings that would disqualify a case from the new category of AML with mutated RUNX1. It tends to occur in older adults without a definite sex predilection. This new provisional disease category appears to represent a biologically distinct group with a possibly worse prognosis than other AML types, and the presence of combined mutations in RUNX1 and ASXL1 appears to be associated with a particularly adverse prognosis.

AML-MRC → now AML, MR

Q. What are the criteria for AML with MDS related changes in WHO5?

 

Essential and desirable diagnostic criteria  

•        Essential: ≥ 20% blasts in blood or marrow;

•        presence of at least one of the following two criteria:

o   (1) a history of MDS or MDS/MPN,

o   (2) one or more cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities listed in below;

•        absence of the following:

o   a history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy, a history of myeloproliferative neoplasm, criteria for AML with defining genetic abnormalities, and criteria for myeloid neoplasms associated with germline predisposition.

What are the morphological criteria for dysplasia in WHO5?

·       Dysgranulopoiesis is characterized by neutrophils with hypogranular cytoplasm, hyposegmented nuclei (pseudo–Pelger–Huët), or unusually segmented nuclei.

·       Dyserythropoiesis is characterized by megaloblastosis and karyorrhexis, as well as nuclear irregularity, fragmentation, or multinucleation. Ring sideroblasts and cytoplasmic vacuoles are additional features of dyserythropoiesis.

·       Dysmegakaryopoiesis is characterized by micromegakaryocytes and normal-sized or large megakaryocytes with non-lobated or multiple separate nuclei.

 

What are the genetic abnormalities that qualify for AML-MR?

·               Complex karyotype (at least three abnormalities)

·               5q deletion or loss of 5q due to unbalanced translocation

·               Monosomy 7, 7q deletion, or loss of 7q due to unbalanced translocation

·               11q deletion

·               12p deletion or loss of 12p due to unbalanced translocation

·               Monosomy 13 or 13q deletion

·               17p deletion or loss of 17p due to unbalanced translocation

·               Isochromosome 17q

·               idic(X)(q13)

 

Cytology provides one of the criteria for recognition of this category of AML (Fig. 15), with clinical history and specific cytogenetic abnormalities also being of relevance. Immunophenotypic features are variable but are those reported in myelodysplastic syndromes, the major anomalies being reduced side scatter reflecting hypogranularity of neutrophils, aberrant differentiation patterns, loss of haematogones, and aberrant expression of CD56 or CD7 [24]. In cases without a preceding myelodysplastic or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm, multilineage dysplasia can suggest the diagnosis but this cannot be confirmed until t(6; 9), mutated NPM1, and biallelic CEBPA mutations are excluded.

 

 

Caveats and Pearls

·       More stringent criteria for dysplasia is required for AML-MRC (≥50% in at least 2 lines) than MDS (≥10%)

·       The presence of significant multilineage dysplasia together with MDS-related cytogenetic defects takes diagnostic precedence over AML, NOS

Q. What is AML with minimal differentiation (M0)?

●      There is no evidence of myeloid differentiation by morphology and light microscopy cytochemistry. (MPO, SBB, naphthol ASD chloroacetate esterase all negative (less than <3% positivity in all blasts))

●      The myeloid nature of the blasts is demonstrated by → immunological markers (CD13+ and CD33+) and/or ultrastructural cytochemistry. Blasts with no granules or few granules.

●      Negative for myelomonocytic differentiation markers (CD11b, CD15, CD14, CD65)

●      Occasional weakly positive for CD7, CD2, CD19 (lymphoid differentiation)

●      Nonspecific genetics: CK, +13, +8, +4, -7

Q. What is AML without maturation (M1)?

●      High percentage of blasts (>/=90% of non-erythroid cells) without significant evidence of maturation to more mature neutrophils.

●      The myeloid nature of the blasts is demonstrated by → MPO and SBB (3%) positivity or Auer rods.

Q. What is AML with maturation (M2)?

●      Acute myeloid leukemia with maturation is characterized by presence of 20% blasts and evidence of maturation (>/=10% of cells are neutrophil lineage).

●      Cells of monocyte lineage are <20%.

●      The arbitrary cutoff of <20% monocytes is what distinguishes this AML from acute myelomonocytic leukemia (M4) (where both neuts and monos are >20% each)

Caveats and Pearls

●      Blasts with azurophilic granules and Auer rods may be seen

●      Blasts may express CD2, CD19

Q. What type of AML is M3?

●      Acute promyelocytic leukemia

Q. What is acute myelomonocytic leukemia (M4)?

●      Rule of 20’s

●      Neutrophils and their precursors and monocytes and their precursors each compromise at least 20% of BM cells.

●      The arbitrary cutoff of 20% monocytes is what distinguishes this from AML with maturation (M2)

Caveats and Pearls

●      Absolute monocytosis may be seen in AMML—not confined to CMML

Q. What is acute monocytic leukemia (M5) - what are the 2 subtypes?

●      M5 requires → 80% or more of the leukemic cells are monocytic

●      Two subtypes are distinguished by the degree of maturation of those monocytic cells

○      1) Acute monoblastic leukemia (M5a) → 80% or more of the leukemic cells are monocytic and the majority (i.e. >80%) are monoblasts as opposed to promonocytes.

○      2) Acute monocytic leukemia (M5b) → 80% or more of the leukemic cells are monocytic lineage. In this type the majority are promonocytes rather than monoblasts.

Caveats and Pearls

●      MPO may be positive in acute monocytic leukemia

 

Q. What is Pure erythroid leukemia (M6)?

●      An acute leukemia where 80% of cells are erythroid precursors with >30% proerythroblasts

Q. What is the history of erythroleukemia

Q. What is the normal erythroid cells immunophenotype?

·       proerythroblasts CD71+ CD105+ CD117+,

·       basophilic erythroblasts CD71+ CD105+ CD117-,

·       polychromatophilic and orthochromatophilic erythroblasts CD71+ CD105- CD117-

 

Q. Summary of Flow Cytometry Findings in AEL in WHO2022:

·       Proerythroblasts: Positive for CD36, CD71, and KIT (CD117)

·       Late erythroid cells: Positive for CD235a (glycophorin A), typically in a KIT-negative subset.

·       CD34: Negative or low in AEL (distinguishing it from myeloblasts in AML).

·       CD45: Dimly positive or variable.

·       HLA-DR: Negative or partially positive.

·       Abnormal markers: CD13 (aberrant expression), CD4 (increased in some cases), and CD38 (decreased in some cases).

Q. What is the typical pattern of Pure red cell aplasia flow cytometry?

·       Absence of CD117 and CD105

 

Caveats and Pearls

·       An erythroid predominant marrow with >20% myeloblasts in the nonerythroid population, but <20% myeloblasts total (previously classified as erythroleukemia; myeloid/erythroid) should be classified as myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts and erythroid predominance

Q. What is Megakaryocytic leukemia (M7)

●      An acute leukemia where 30% of cells are blasts; some show budding

●      Megakaryoblasts → PAS and NSE positive.

●      Megakaryoblasts are CD41 and 61 positive, classically CD 36+ and MPO –

●      Note → cytoplasmic CD41 and 61 is most specific

●      Note: WHO says “>/=20% blasts, of which >/=50% are of megakaryocyte lineage”

Acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis → not in WHO 2022/ICC

 

What is the differential for acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis?

 

This entity is distinct and needs to be distinguished from:

●      1) Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7)

●      2) AML with myelodysplasia related changes (AML-MRC)

●      3) Myelodysplastic syndrome - refractory anemia with excess blast II (MDS-RAEB-II) with fibrosis

●      4) Primary myelofibrosis (PMF)

Q. What are the morphologic findings in acute panmyelosis - 3 key findings?

  1. Hypercellular marrow → with panmyelosis
  2. Fibrosis → marked increase in reticulin fibres (though frank collagenous fibrosis is rare)
  3. Dysplasia → conspicuously dysplastic megakaryocytes

Q. What is the median blast count in panmyelosis?

●      22.5%

Q. What is important to note about the immunophenotype of acute panmyelosis?

●      Blasts usually have a progenitor associated immunophenotype

●      Positive → CD34 with other immature markers like CD117, CD13, CD33

●      Negative → typically MPO negative and don't have megakaryocytic markers (helps differentiate between a M7)

Q. How do you use cytogenetics to classify acute panmyelosis - what is the key alternative diagnosis that CGs may indicate?

●      If there is a complex karyotype you classify it as → AML with myelodysplasia related changes (AML-MRC) and not acute panmyelosis.

 

ACUTE PROMYELOCYTIC LEUKEMIA

 

Q. What is the classic APL immunophenotype?

 

Classic APL phenotype:

●      Negative → CD34 negative/partial or weak positive, HLA-DR negative (the only AML that is negative), CD11b negative (integrins), CD15 weak or negative (normal promyelocytes are CD15 positive)

●      Positive → CD13 positive, CD33 positive, CD117 weak/variable (CD117 indicates immaturity in the absence of CD34)

●      Aberrant lineage expression → sometimes CD2 positive (with CD34 positive in microgranular variant) and CD56 positive

●      Similar to normal promyelocytes except → for the abnormally low levels of CD117 and CD15

Q. What is the most common variant of APL and is it responsive to retinoids?

●      ZBTB16-RARA aka PLZF/RARa and t(11;17) → a variant translocation t(11;17)(q23;q21.1) has been described in approximately 1% of patients with APL.

●      Although the number of cases studied is small, APL with t(11;17)(q23;q21.1) is usually refractory to therapy with retinoids.

Q. Are the other common variants in APL response to ATRA?

●      ZBTB16/PLZF, and STAT5B is → resiZStant

●      NPM1/RARa t(5;17) and NUMA/RARa t(11;17) are both → respoNsive

Q. What antigen expression is microgranular variant APL uniquely associated with - 2 markers?

●      CD34 and CD2 positive

●      These antigens are also seen with the bcr3 transcript of the PML-RARA fusion gene.

●      Higher WCC

Q. Expression of what antigen is associated with poor outcome in APL?

●      CD56.

●      It is expressed in 20% of cases.

Q. What are 3 morphologic variants in APL?

●      Hypergranular form (75% of cases)

●      Microgranular form (hypogranular) (25% of cases)

●      Variant t(11;17) ZBTB16/PLZF-RARa (CD13+, CD56+, no Auer rods, pelgeroid PMNs)

Q. What are the morphologic features of the t(11;17) ZBTB16/PLZF-RARA APL?

●      Cells with the variant translocation t(11;17) tend to have → nuclei that are more regular in outline, with an increased number of maturing neutrophils with hypolobation (ie, acquired Pelger-Huet anomaly & absence of Auer rods.

●      These cases have features intermediate between AML with maturation and APL → with sparser granules, lack of faggot cells, and absence of the typical bilobed nucleus seen in the typical forms of APL

Q. What are 3 types of AML that most commonly have FLT3 mutations?

●      AML with t(6;9)

●      Normal karyotype

●      APL (~40% FLT3 followed by WT1, NRAS)( High risk of relapse in FLT3-ITD- or FLT3-TKD-mutated APL cases)

●      (also inv(16) have 20% FLT3-ITD)

 

Q. What is “ATRA”?

●      All Trans Retinoic Acid

 

Q What are the Clinical findings in ATRA syndrome aka APL differentiation syndrome.

·       Fever

·       Acute Respiratory Distress

·       Pulmonary Infiltrates

·       Pleural/pericardial effusion

·       Vascular capillary leak syndrome (hypotension, weight gain, fluid retention)

·       Renal failure

·       Fluid overload/peripheral edema

·       Weight gain >5kg

·       Unexplained hypotension

Q. List 5 laboratory findings of tumor lysis syndrome TLS?

a.     Hyperkalemia

b.     Hyperphosphatemia

c.     Hypocalcemia

d.     High uric acid

e.     (Uremia) Azotemia

f.       lactic Acidosis

The first four [K, phos, uric high, ca low] are the classical lab findings

For your reference: there are three risk groups for TLS

1.     High risk (>5% risk for TLS)

2.     Intermediate risk (1-5% risk)

3.     Low risk (<1%)

 

Transfusion threshold in APL

·       National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) goals for supportive measures include hemoglobin (Hgb) > 8 g/dL, platelet counts > 50 × 109/L, fibrinogen > 150 mg/dL, and PT (sec) and PTT (sec) values close to normal

 

Q. What is “ATO”?

●      Arsenic trioxide

Q. What is the treatment of high-risk APL (initial WBC count >10 x 109/L)?

●      ATRA plus anthracycline-based chemotherapy (Idarubicin is classic) remains the recommended initial therapy (without ATO) for high-risk APL until more data are available regarding the early use of ATO in this small subset.

Q. What is the treatment of low or intermediate-risk APL (initial WBC count ≤ 10 x 109/L)?

●      ATRA plus ATO rather than ATRA plus anthracycline-based chemotherapy.

Q. What are 4 ways the molecular lesions in APL be identified?

●      Conventional karyotype

●      Fluorescence in situ hybridization FISH

●      Reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction RT-PCR

●      Anti-PML monoclonal antibodies (IHC)

Q. How useful is ATO?

●      Arsenic trioxide (ATO), alone or in combination with ATRA, is capable of producing complete remissions

Key Differences:

  1. CD2 and CD34 Expression:
    • Hypogranular APL shows significantly higher CD2⁺ (80% vs. 3.1%) and CD34⁺ (75% vs. 4.1%) expression.
    • This reflects a more immature immunophenotype in the hypogranular variant.
  2. CD64 Expression:
    • Hypogranular APL has a higher frequency of CD64 expression (80%) compared to hypergranular APL (57.5%).
  3. Side Scatter:
    • Hypergranular APL exhibits a markedly increased side scatter (reflecting granularity), while hypogranular APL has low side scatter (consistent with blasts).

 

 

Therapy-related myeloid neoplasms

Q. What are the different types of “Therapy Related Myeloid Neoplasms”; What is excluded?

●      Includes → therapy related MDS, AML, and MDS/MPN

●      Excludes → progression of pre-existing MPN, MDS, or MDS/MPN to AML. As in each of these cases there is a natural progression to AML and it’s not possible to distinguish natural progression from therapy induced changes

Q. What agents have been associated with therapy related AML - 4 groups (give 3 egs of each)?

●      1) Alkylating agents

○      Cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, carboplatin, cisplatin, mitomycin C, etc

○      Think of drugs starting with “C”

●      2) Topoisomerase II inhibitors

○      Etoposide, teniposide, daunorubicin, doxorubicin, mitoxantrone

○      Think of “to, po, no, xo”

●      3) Ionizing radiation

○      Large fields including active bone marrow

●      4) Others

○      Antitubulin agents (vincristine and vinblastine)

○      Antimetabolites (fludarabine, thiopurines, mycophenolate)

 

Q. What are the 2 clinical subtypes of t-Myeloid Neoplasms?

●      1) Early → 1 - 5 year post topoisomerase II inhibitor use.

○      Represents 20-30% of cases.

○      Associated with overt acute leukemia

○      Associated with balanced chromosomal translocations involving 11q23 (KMT2A) or 21q22 (RUNX1).

●      2) Late → 5 -10 years post alkylating agents and/or ionizing radiation.

○      More gradual and insidious onset

○      Presents clinically with preceding MDS and bone marrow failure.

○      Have unbalanced loss of genetic material typically involving chromosome 5 or 7 as well as complex karyotypes and mutations or loss of TP53.

 

Q. What are the predictive factors in t-AML? 

●      Significance of therapy is not entirely clear.

●      The outcome is strongly influenced by → cytogenetic risk profile

●      CG profile is typically adverse given high incidence of involving chromosome 5, 7, and complex karyotypes.

●      In some balanced translocations they have worse prognosis than de novo counterparts except inv(16), t(16;16), and APL.

 

Caveats and Pearls

·       This category does not apply to cases of MPN with prior therapy

·       This category trumps all other alternative myeloid neoplasm designations, such as acute promyelocytic leukemia and AML with t(9;11)

What clinical features should make you consider a Myeloid Neoplasm with Germline Predisposition? Give 5 specific examples       

 

Any patient presenting with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) or acute leukaemia, i.e. acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) or lymphoblastic leukaemia, with any of the following:

  • A personal history of multiple cancers
  • Thrombocytopenia, bleeding propensity, or macrocytosis preceding the diagnosis of MDS/AML by several years
  • A first- or second-degree relative with a haematological neoplasm
  • A first- or second-degree relative with a solid tumour consistent with germline predisposition; i.e. sarcoma, early-onset breast cancer (at patient age <50 years), or brain tumours
  • Abnormal nails or skin pigmentation, oral leukoplakia, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, unexplained liver disease, lymphoedema, atypical infections, immune deficiencies, congenital limb anomalies, or short stature (in the patient or a first- or second-degree relative)

Any healthy potential haematopoietic stem cell donor who is planning to donate for a family member with a haematological malignancy with any of the conditions listed above or who fails to mobilize stem cells well using standard protocols.

 

CEBPA

What is the morphology and immunophenotype of AML with mutated CEBPA          

 

●      Similar morphology and immunophenotype to sporadic CEBPA mutations

●      Morphology:

○      Predominance of AML without maturation

○      Presence of Auer rods

●      Immunophenotype

○      Frequent aberrant CD7

●      Normal karyotype

●      Second allele mutations are common, typically at the 3′ end

●      Myeloid malignancies are relatively chemosensitive

●      Without allogeneic stem cell transplant, individuals are susceptible to additional independent malignancies (not relapses)

 

DDX41

What is unique about the development of myeloid neoplasms with germline DDX41 mutation? What is the prognosis?

 

●      Autosomal dominant familial MDS/AML

●      Inherited mutations on Chr 5 encoding gene DDX41 = Dead box RNA helicase

●      Significant subset of cases with Biallelic DDX41 (one germline, one somatic)

●      Associated with long latency = unique feature

○      Mean patient age of 62 years

●      Penetrance not fully established, appears high

●      Poor prognosis

●      Initially better than favorable and intermediate/adverse groups but later catchup and become worse than them

●     

BM findings in germline DDX41 mutation - 1 unique feature?  What type of AML may develop?

 

●      Usually leukopenia

●      Hypocellular BM with prominent erythroid dysplasia

●      Often leading to → erythroid leukemia

●      Normal karyotype

RUNX1

What is RUNX1?          

 

●      RUNX1 (Chr 21) = core binding transcription factor regulating expression of several genes essential for hematopoiesis

What is the clinical presentation of RUNX1 germline mutation?          

 

●      Familial platelet disorder with variable presentation even within a family

●      11-100% risk of myeloid neoplasm development

●      MDS/AML likely requires additional mutations

●      Bleeding phenotype:

○      Mild to moderate bleeding tendency in some

○      May have no bleeding history

●      Platelets:

○      Platelet count = normal or mildly decreased

○      Platelet morphology = Normal

○      Platelet function

■      i) Most have impaired platelet aggregation with Collagen and Epinephrine

■      ii) Can have dense granule storage pool disorder

●      Associated with lifelong thrombocytopenia and qualitative platelet defects, T-ALL and (more rarely) B-cell malignancies

ANKRD26

What is the pathogenesis of Myeloid Neoplasms with germline ANKRD26 Mutation?          

 

●      Most mutations occur within 5' untranslated region and disrupt assembly of RUNX1 and FLI1 on the ANKRD26 promoter

●      Result in → increased gene transcription and signaling through MPL pathway

●      Leads to impaired protoplatelet formation

●      30x higher incidence of AML/MDS

●      No syndromic features

●      Thrombocytopenia

●      Variable platelet function abnormalities

Clinical presentation of Myeloid Neoplasms with germline ANKRD26 Mutation?          

 

●      30x higher incidence of AML/MDS

●      Platelet count: Variable

●      Mostly moderate thrombocytopenia with normal platelet size

●      Platelet function:

○      GP1a and alpha granule defect common

○      In vitro platelet studies often normal

●      TPO often elevated

●      Mild bleeding tendencies

Abnormal morphology of what cell type may be seen in the BM of Myeloid Neoplasms with germline ANKRD26 Mutation?          

 

●      Funny looking megakaryocytes

●      Dysmegakaryopoiesis in small number of patients without leukemia

●      MK increased in number and have → small hyposegmented nuclei, bilobed nuclei or micromegas

ETV6

●      Autosomal Dominant Thrombocytopenia and hematological neoplasms

●      Variable thrombocytopenia with normal sized platelets

●      Mild to moderate bleeding tendency

GATA2

Name 2 physiological processes regulated by GATA2 transcription factor   

 

●      GATA2 = zinc-finger transcription factor regulating hematopoeisis, autoimmunity and inflammatory and developmental processes

●      Mono-allelic Germline GATA2 mutations in both coding and non-coding regions

○      Missense, null, and regulatory mutations resulting in loss of function/ haploinsufficiency

●      Lymphoedema and severe infections common in null mutations

●      Associated with immunodeficiencies, lymphoedema, and many other phenotypes

Germline GATA2 mutations were originally identified as what 4 separate syndromes?          

 

  1. MonoMac syndrome
    - Monocytopenia and non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection
  2. Dendritic Cell, monocyte, B- and NK-lymphoid (DCML) deficiency with vulnerability to viral infections
  3. Familial MDS/AML
  4. Emberger syndrome, characterized by primary lymphoedema, warts and predisposition to MDS/AML

Note: GATA2 mutations also recognized in congenital neutropenia and aplastic anemia

Name 1 concurrent mutation & 1 CG abnormality that may be seen together with GATA2 Mutations          

 

●      Concurrent ASXL1 mutations seen in many patients with monosomy 7

What is the likelihood of developing AML/MDS with GATA2 germline mutations?          

 

●      70% of individuals develop MDS/AML

●      Median age 29 years

Name 2 other CG abnormalities associated with GATA2 mutations          

 

●      Highly prevalence of Monosomy 7 (37%)

●      Trisomy 8

 

Bone marrow failure syndrome

Name 4 BM failure syndromes associated with AML/MDS          

 

●      1. Fanconi Anemia FA

●      2. Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome SDS

●      3. Diamond-Blackfan Anemia DBA

●      4. Severe congenital Neutropenia SCN

●      Note: another associated disorder that is not a BM failure syndrome = telomere biology disorders (dyskeratosis congenita)

What are the Genes associated with Fanconi Anemia FA (and inheritance Patterns) - Name 5          

 

●      ABCD (1 & 2) EFG

●      Autosomal Recessive:

●      FANCA, FANCC,
- BRCA2 (FANCD1)
- FANCD2, FANCE, FANCF, FANCG, FANCI,
- BRIP1 (FANCJ), FANCL, FANCM, FANCN

●      X-linked:
- FANCB

●      Autosomal Dominant

○      FANCR

What are the phenotypic findings of Fanconi Anemia FA - List 5 features          

 

●      1. Bone Marrow Failure

●      2. Low birth weight

●      3. Short stature

●      4. Radial anomalies - (abnormal thumbs, absent radii)

●      5. Congenital heart disease

●      6. Microphthalmia

●      7. Ear anomalies, deafness

●      8. Renal manifestations

●      9. Hypogonadism

●      10. Cafe au lait spots

●      11. Solid tumours

●      12. Predisposition for myeloId malignancy - (AML 9%, MDS 7%)

List the 3 possible inheritance patterns and affected genes associated with Severe Congenital Neutropenia (SCN) - Mention at least 1 gene for each inheritance pattern          

 

●      Autosomal Dominant:

○      ELANE, CSF3R, GFI1

●      Autosomal Recessive

○      HAX1, G6PC3

●      X-linked Recessive

○      WAS

List 1 unique clinical/phenotypic finding associated with HAX1 & G6PC3 gene mutations in SCN          

 

●      HAX1:

○      Neurodevelopmental

●      G6PC3:

○      Cardiac and other

○      Up to 40% risk of MDS/AML

●      Autosomal Recessive
SBDS gene

●      MDS, AML, ALL

List 4 characteristic phenotypic findings associated with Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome SDS         

 

●      1. Preceding isolated neutropenia

List 3 gene mutations and 2 inheritance patterns associated with Diamond Blackfan Anemia DBA

What are the 3 hematological neoplasms associated with Diamond-Blackfan Anemia DBA

What are 3 phenotypic features of patients with Diamond Blackfan Anemia DBA?

Ch8 –Myeloid proliferations associated with Down syndrome (MLADS)

Q: What is Transient Abnormal Myelopoiesis (TAM) in newborns with Down syndrome?

·       Newborn with thrombocytopenia and circulating megakaryoblasts

·       Spontaneous resolution within 3 months

·       20–30% progress to AML within 3 years

 

Q: What is the clinical presentation of myeloid leukemia in children with Down Syndrome?

·       Young child (<5 years) with thrombocytopenia and MDS or acute megakaryoblastic leukemia

 

Q: What are the key morphological features of TAM?

·       Megakaryoblasts in blood and marrow

·       Erythroid and megakaryocytic dysplasia

 

Q: What immunophenotypic markers are positive in TAM and AML associated with Down syndrome?

·       POSITIVE: CD41, CD42b, CD61, CD71, CD117, CD34 (TAM > AML)

 

Q: Which immunophenotypic markers are typically negative in TAM and AML associated with Down syndrome?

·       NEGATIVE: MPO, glycophorin A, CD14

 

Q: What genetic mutations and abnormalities are commonly associated with myeloid proliferations in Down syndrome?

·       GATA1 mutations

·       Trisomy 8

·       Trisomy 21 (constitutional)

 

Q: What is the primary differential diagnosis for myeloid leukemia in children with Down syndrome?

  • Conventional pediatric MDS/AML, particularly in children older than 5 years who are GATA1-negative.

 

Q. What is the most common type of AML in DS?          

·       Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia: 70% in <4 years old with down syndrome. (3-6% in kids without down syndrome)

 

Why is AML in DS recognized as a distinct entity?          

·       Because the acute megakaryoblastic leukemia that occur in DS has unique morphological, immunophenotypic, molecular genetic and clinical characteristics → that distinguish it from other forms of acute megakaryocytic leukemias including GATA1 mutations.

Q. Should all cases of AML and ALL in DS be classified as myeloid leukemia with down syndrome?          

·       No → cases with AML and ALL in down syndrome should NOT be automatically classified as myeloid leukemia with down syndrome.

·       For eg, cases that meet the criteria for leukemic disorders not associated with down syndrome should be classified as such

 

Q. What is TAM?          

 

TAM = Transient Abnormal Myelopoiesis → a transient myeloproliferative disorder

 

-        Unique disorder of newborns with DS that → presents with clinical and morphological findings indistinguishable from those of AML.

-        Note this arises from fetal-liver hematopoietic cells!

The blasts have morphological and immunological features of megakaryocytic lineage.

Q. What is the clinical course of TAM?          

·       Spontaneous remission within → first 3 months of life.

·       Few children may experience life-threatening or fatal clinical complications

 

Q. Mention some of clinical features of TAM?          

·       Diagnosed shortly after birth → at age 3-7 days

·       Some are asymptomatic and diagnosed later

·       Thrombocytopenia = most common, other cytopenias are less common

·       Leukocytosis maybe present

·       Blasts in PB may exceed blasts in BM

·       Hepatosplenomegaly

·       Less common: Jaundice, ascites, respiratory distress, bleeding, pericardial effusion

·       Rare clinical complications of TAM: skin rash, cardiopulmonary failure,hyperviscosity, splenic necrosis renal failure, hydrops fetalis and progressive hepatic necrosis.

Describe the morphological features of TAM ?          

·       -PB and BM blasts: basophilic cytoplasm with coarse basophilic granules and cytoplasmic blebs suggestive of megakaryoblasts

·       -Some have PB basophilia

·       -Erythroid and megakaryocytic dysplasia

What is the immunophenotype of TAM?          

·       -Positive: CD34, KIT (CD117), CDD13, CD33, HLA-DR, CD4(dim), CD41, CD42, CD110 (TPO receptor), IL3R, CD36, CD61, and CD71

·       -Negative for: MPO, CD15, CD14, CD11a, and glycophorin A.

·       -IHC: CD41, CD61, CD42b

What 2 markers are aberrantly expressed in TAM?    

·       CD7 and CD56

What is the hallmark genetic mutation in TAM and its effect?          

·       Acquired GATA1 mutations are present in blast cells of TAM

·       GATA1 = a transcription factor
The mutation results in truncated protein that promotes →  megakaryocytic proliferation.

·       GATA1 associated with X-Linked Thrombocytopenia with or without dyserythropoiesis, DS-AML, DBA

What is the indication of chemotherapy in TAM?          

·       Treatment for life-threatening hepatic, renal or cardiac failure is sometimes necessary.


Is there any biological difference between AML and MDS in DS?           

·       No biological differences between MDS or overt AML

·       A comparable diagnostic differentiation algorithm has no prognostic or therapeutic implications

What are the morphological features of AML in DS?          

 

PB:
-Blasts and occasionally erythroid precursors are usually present
-Anisopoikilocytosis And dacrocytes
-Thrombocytopenia and giant platelets

BM aspirate:
-Blasts: distinctive features: round to slightly irregular nuclei and a moderate amount of basophilic cytoplasm ,cytoplasmic blebs
The cytoplasm contains large coarse granules resembling basophilic granules. The granules are MPO-negative

-Erythroid: megaloblastic changes and dysplastic forms including binucleated or tri nucleated cells and nuclear fragments

-Dysgranulopoiesis may present

 BM biopsy:

-dense reticulin fibrosis making BM aspiration difficult or impossible
-Erythropoiesis may be increased in cases with low blast percentage and decreases with disease progression
-Maturing cells of granulocytic lineage are usually decreased
Rare dysplastic megas can be seen in cases with a dense blast cell infiltrate
In other cases, megas can be markedly increased with clusters of dysplastic small forms and micromegas

What is the immunophenotype in AML with DS?          

 

Blasts in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia associated with DS:

Positive → KIT, CD13, CD33, CD11b, CD7, CD4, CD42, CD110, CD36, IL-3R, CD41, CD61 and CD71

Negative → MPO, CD15, CD14, and glycophorin A

Unlike TAM → CD34 negative in 50% of cases and 30% of cases are negative for CD56 and CD41

Q. What it the pathognomic mutation in AML/MDS with DS?          

 

GATA1 mutation.

Children >5 years with myeloid leukemia may not have GATA1 mutations and such cases should be considered conventional MDS or AML

Leukemia appears to arise from GATA1-mutated TAM clone that has acquired additional mutations including CTCF, EZH2, KANSL1, JAK2, JAK3, MPL, SH2B3 and RAS pathway genes

 

What is the most common cytogenetic abnormality?          

 

Trisomy 8 13-44%

Is monosomy 7 common in AML with DS?          

 

No → it is rare.

What is the prognosis of AML with DS compared to AML with no DS?          

 

- Very favourable prognosis compared with that AML without DS
- Better response to treatment in cases with GATA1 mutations

- Treatment should be done with Down syndrome-specific protocols
- Myeloid leukemia in older children with DS with GATA1 mutation has a poorer prognosis, comparable to that of AML in patients without DS.

 

Ch8 –Myeloid sarcoma (MS)

Q. What is the definition of Myeloid sarcoma?          

·       A tumor mass consisting of myeloid blasts with or without maturation.

·       Occurring at anatomical site other than the bone marrow.

·       Infiltration of any site of the body by myeloid blasts in a patient with leukemia is → NOT classified as myeloid sarcoma UNLESS it presents with tumour masses in which the tissue architecture is affected.

·       Its detection is equivalent of a diagnosis of AML

Q. What are the most commonly affected sites in myeloid sarcoma          

·       LNs, GI, bone and soft tissue and testes

Q. What is the percentage of cases that occur as isolated myeloid sarcoma with absence of underlying AML or other myeloid neoplasms          

·       25%

Q. What is the morphology of myeloid sarcoma in lymph nodes and extranodal sites?          

·       In LNs → either infiltrate the paracortex surrounding the reactive follicles or grows diffusely, often extending into the perinodal fat.

·       In extranodal sites → mimics metastatic carcinoma by forming cohesive nests and/or single files surrounded by fibrotic septa.

Q. Mention 3 of the AML recurrent genetic translocations that can be detected in Myeloid sarcoma?          

·       t(8;21)

·       inv(16)

·       t(9;11)

 

Q. What chromosomal aberrations can be seen in approximately 50% of cases of myeloid sarcoma          

·       55% of cases

·       Monosomies: 7, 16, loss of 16q,5q or 20q

·       Trisomies: 8, 4, 11

·       KMT2A rearrangement, inv(16)

Caveats and Pearls

·       Myeloid sarcoma may express BPDCN markers CD4, CD56, and CD123

·       Myeloid sarcoma may express TdT and aberrantly express cytokeratin and/or lymphoid markers

Ch9 – Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN)

Q. What are the 3 types of clinical presentation of BPDCNs with skin lesions?         

 

●      1) An isolated (one or few) → purplish nodule type

○      ⅔ of cases

○      Found preferentially on the head and lower limbs and can be >10cm in diameter

●      2) An isolated (one or few) → bruise-like papule type

○      Clinically very challenging

●      3) Disseminated type → with purplish nodules and/or papules and/or macules

Q. What are clinical features of BPDCN other than cutaneous?         

 

●      Regional lymphadenopathy at presentation is common (20% of cases)

●      PB and BM involvement can be minimal at presentation, invariably develops with progression of disease

○      Cytopenias: esp thrombocytopenia

●      Oral mucosal infiltration: can be seen

 

Q. What % of BPDCN is associated with or develop into what 3 myeloid neoplasm 

 

●      10-20%

●      CMML, MDS, AML

Q. Describe the blasts in BPDCN?         

 

●      Nonspecific blasts

○      Diffuse monomorphous infiltrate

○      Medium-sized blast cells resembling → lymphoblast or myeloblasts

●      Nuclei have irregular contours, fine chromatin and one to several small nucleoli

●      Cytoplasm: scant and appears greyish blue and agranular on Giemsa staining

 



Q. What are the morphological features of BPDCN in cutaneous, Lymph nodes and BM biopsy and aspirate?         

 

●      Cutaneous:
-Dermis is massively involved with extension to the subcutaneous fat
-The epidermis and adnexa are spared (no epidermotropism)

●      LNs:
-Diffusely involved in the interfollicular areas and medulla
-B cell follicles are often spared

●      BM biopsy:
-A mild interstitial infiltrate (detectable only by IHC) OR massive replacement
-Residual hematopoiesis may exhibit dysplastic changes especially in megas.

○      https://imagebank.hematology.org/getimagebyid/60358?size=3

○      https://imagebank.hematology.org/getimagebyid/60359?size=3

●      In PB and BM aspirate:
 -tumor cells may show cytoplasmic microvacuoles localized along the cell membrane and pseudopodia
-Granules and crystals are absent

○      https://imagebank.hematology.org/getimagebyid/60354?size=3

●      Angioinvasion and coagulative necrosis are absent

 

Q. What transcription factor is a diagnostic marker for BPDCN and is essential to drive PDCs development         

 

●      TCF4

Q. What is the unique phenotype of BPDCNs (pathognomic)        

 

●      The absence of lineage-associated antigens

●      Positivity for → CD45RA, CD123, CD4, CD56 (Mnemonic “123, 4, 56”)

●      CD303, TCL1[QZ3] A, CD2AP

●      CD43 +

●      CD34 - (note: can be + by flow in 17%)

●      Can be CD117 and TdT +

●      EBV -

Q.  What marker can be a therapeutic target in BPDCNs?         

 

●      CD123

●      Tagraxofusp FDA approved

●      TAG(target therapy) RAX O FUSP

●      CD123-directed cytotoxin consisting of human interleukin-3 fused to truncated diphtheria toxin

●      BCL2 antagonist - venetoclax


Q. What is the most commonly mutated gene in BPDCN         

 

●      TET2 and ASXL1

Q. Mention some of the genetic mutations in BPDCNs?         

 

●      TET2, NPM1, NRAS, KRAS, ATM, MET, IDH2, KIT, APC, RB1, BRAF, TP53

●      ASXL1, RAS family genes, IKZF3, ZEB2

Q. What chemotherapy protocol is more effective in treating BPDCNs? ALL or AML protocols         

 

●      ALL

○      Lymphoblastic leukemia chemotherapy seems to be more effective than AML oriented chemo

■      May be due to deregulation of several genes in common with ALL resulting in higher sensitivity to drug

○      Allo SCT is recommended after first complete remission

 

Q. How would you differentiate mature plasmacytoid dendritic cell proliferation (MPDCP) from BPDCNs?         

Mature plasmacytoid dendritic cell proliferation (MPDCP):

●      PDCs are mature

●      CD56 is negative or show focal or weak reactivity

●      Low Ki67 proliferation index <10%

●      Negative TdT

Q. What is the difference between macrophages and histiocytes?

●      DCs, monocytes, and macrophages are members of the mononuclear phagocyte system.

●      Histiocyte is a morphological term referring to tissue-resident macrophages.

●      Macrophages are large ovoid cells mainly involved in the clearance of apoptotic cells, debris, and pathogens.

 

Q. What is blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) - precursor cell?

●      Aggressive tumor derived from precursors of plasmacytoid dendritic cells[QZ5] .

 Q. 3 most common tissue types involved by BPDCN?

●      Most commonly involves skin (64-100%), bone marrow (60-90%), and lymph nodes (40-50%).

Q. What 2 myeloid malignancies may BPDCN transform into?

●      10-20% of cases develop into CMML or AML.

●      Association with this disease and MDS is uncertain but appears to a be a link as these secondary neoplasms are felt to arise from underlying MDS at time of diagnosis.

●      Negative [QZ6] → notably other lineage specific markers are negative = CD3 (T), CD19 (B) and MPO (myeloid) are all negative

Ch10 – Acute leukemias of ambiguous lineage

Q. What are the criteria for “acute Leukemias of ambiguous lineage, NOS”?

●      Blasts express combinations of markers that do not allow their classification as either

○      1) Acute undifferentiated leukemias or

○      2) Mixed phenotype acute leukemias as defined in WHO

Q. What are the possible scenarios that qualify as categorization as a “mixed phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL)”?

 

Possible scenarios:

●      1) Two distinct populations of leukemic cells → each independently meets criteria for either AML, T-cell ALL, or B-cell ALL (though each blast population doesn’t need to be above 20% and blasts are defined as you typically define them)

●      2) One dominant blast population with blasts expressing markers from 2 lineages

○      Caveat → This immunophenotype definition of B-cells ONLY applies in MPAL.

○      CD19 Brightness is defined relative to normal B-cells.

○      Caveat → a number of normal B-cell ALL cases have been identified with weak MPO expression by flow. These cases should not be diagnosed as MPAL and should be considered B-cell ALL.

Q. What are the lineage criteria used to assign MPAL when a single blast population is present?

●      Myeloid Lineage:

○      MPO, or

○      Monocytic differentiation (2 or more of: NSE, lysozyme, CD11c, CD14, CD64)

●      T-cell lineage:

○      cCD3 (epsilon) or surface CD3 (rare in MPAL)

○      intensity in part exceeds 50% of mature T-cells level by FCM or,

○      immunocytochemistry positive with non-zeta chain reagent

●      B-cell lineage:

○      1) Strong CD19 and 1 or more of strong CD79a, CD22, or CD10

○      2) Weak CD19 and 2 or more of strong CD79a, CD22, or CD10

Strong: CD19 intensity in part exceeds 50% of normal B cell progenitor by flow cytometry.

Weak: CD19 intensity does not exceed 50% of normal B cell progenitor by flow cytometry.

CD79a: CD79a should not be used in differential with T lineage

 

Q.    What are the 4 recurring genetic abnormalities defining ICC 2022 and WHO-HAEM5 ALAL genetic entities?

  • MPAL with BCR::ABL1 fusion
  • MPAL with t(v;11q23.3), KMT2A rearranged
  • MPAL with ZNF384 rearrangement
  • MPAL/ALAL with BCL11B rearrangement

 

Q. What are the 2 specific translocations that may be seen with MPAL?

●      MPAL with t(9;22)

●      MPAL with t(v;11q23);KMT2A-rearranged

 

Q. What age groups do BCR::ABL1 and KMT2A MPAL see?

●      BCR::ABL1 fusion MPAL most common in adults

●      KMT2A-rearranged, ZNF384-rearranged MPAL more common in pediatric population

 

Q. What are the criteria for “MPAL with t(9;22)”?

 

●      Diagnosis requires 2 things:

○      1) Criteria for MPAL are met

○      2) The presence of t(9;22)

●      If patient has an established diagnosis of CML preceding this → do NOT call it MPAL, it should be considered → blast crisis CML.

●      No history of exposure to cytotoxic therapy.

Q. what should you exclude before diagnosing MPAL BCR::ABL1?

 

●      Per ICC 2022 and WHO-HAEM5: Exclude cases with either history of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) or presenting as CML in blast phase

●      Per WHO-HAEM5: Exclude acquiring BCR::ABL1 secondarily at later time during disease course

 

Q. What is “MPAL with t(v;11q23);KMT2A-rearranged” - what alternative diagnosis must you consider when making this diagnosis?

 

●      Diagnosis requires 2 things:

○      Criteria for MPAL are met

○      Presence of KMT2A translocation (previously known as MLL)

●      DDx → t(v;11q23) is a common translocation in B-cell ALL and commonly has myeloid markers so do NOT call it MPAL unless strict criteria are met.

B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma

 

Q. For B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma what is the distinction between the terms “leukemia vs lymphoma”?

●      The term lymphoma → is used when the disease is confined to a mass lesion with no or minimal evidence of blood or bone marrow involvement.

●      There is no definitive blast count required to meet the criteria for “leukemia” in ALL

●      25% = commonly used for studies

●      WHO cautions against diagnosing lymphoblastic leukemia with counts <20%

Q. Sites of involvement by B-ALL vs B-LBL?

●      B-ALL commonly involves:

○      Blood & BM

○      Lymph nodes

○      Spleen

○      Liver

○      CNS

○      Testes

●      B-LBL commonly presents in:

○      Lymph Nodes

○      Skin

○      Soft tissue

○      Bone

 

Q. How to diagnose B-ALL?

●      Blast cutoffs

○      There is no definitive blast count required.

○      25% commonly used for studies

○      WHO cautions against diagnosing with counts <20%.

●      Lineage assignment

○      B-cell lineage is defined by immunophenotype

○      Flow cytometry → is therefore the cornerstone of diagnosing Lymphoid neoplasms.

Q. B-ALL Immunophenotype?

●      No single specific marker

●      Generally positive for CD19, cCD79a (sensitive and specific), and cCD22(very sensitive) → none are specific, and diagnosis is usually made from a combination of markers present or bright expression.

●      Typically expressed → CD10(not all), CD22(weak but consistent), CD24, PAX5(more specific than CD79a), and TdT.

●      Variable expression → CD34 and CD20

●      Dim or absent → CD45 (downregulated; failed to express in 10-20%)

●      Ewing sarcoma may resemble LBL: CD99 positive in ES also express in by most hematopoietic tumors that express TdT → expression of CD99/lack of CD45 does not exclude LBL

●      Note: TdT = Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) → a specialized DNA polymerase expressed in immature, pre-B, pre-T lymphoid cells, and acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma cells. Marker of immaturity for lymphoblasts. 10% of AML too

pre B ALL cells characteristically coexpress CD10 and CD19. In addition, CD20 and CD23 (other B cell markers) are not expressed.

Expression of CD34 and TdT indicates immaturity and is characteristic in pre B ALL. cytoplasmic expression of CD79 confirms B cell lineage.

CD38 is an expression of immaturity. The ploidy as seen by the DNA Histogram, indicates a hypodiploidy (DI=0.53) indicating poor prognosis.

 

Q. The degree of differentiation of B-ALL can be assessed by immunophenotype?

●      Earliest stage blasts express CD19, cytoplasmic CD79a, cytoplasmic CD22, and TdT; such B-ALLs occur in infancy

●      Intermediate-stage blasts express CD10, CD19, surface CD79a, surface CD22, and TdT

●      Most mature-stage blasts express cytoplasmic μ chains (c-μ), CD34 often (-)

●      The old answer is hidden[QZ7] 

●      Pro-B -> Common -> Pre-B -> Mature B

Q. What about surface light chain expression - is it present or absent in B-ALL?

●      WHO states “clonal surface immunoglobulin light chain is characteristically absent, although its presence does not exclude the possibility of B-ALL/LBL”

●      But what does WHO cite as evidence?

○      In classic WHO fashion they cite a paper which has nothing to do with their statement.

○      They cite a case report of 5 cases of Burkitt lymphoma which are negative for surface light chain.

Q. In a case of suspected B-ALL, if light chain expression is present → what alternative diagnosis should you consider?

 

Think high grade lymphomas:

●      Burkitt lymphoma

●      High-grade lymphoma (Double HIT or Triple HIT)

●      High-grade B-cell lymphoma, NOS

●      DLBCL

Q. But surely there is a case report somewhere of B-ALL with surface LC expression (there are case reports for everything)?

●      There is, see Surface immunoglobulin light chain-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia of FAB L1 or L2 Type A Report of 6 Cases in Adults. (Vasef MA, Brynes RK, Murata-Collins JL, Arber DA, Medeiros LJ. Surface immunoglobulin light chain-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia of FAB L1 or L2 type: a report of 6 cases in adults. Am J Clin Pathol. 1998 Aug;110(2):143-9. doi: 10.1093/ajcp/110.2.143. PMID: 9704611.)

Q. What antigen cross expression is seen commonly in B-ALL?

●      Myeloid antigens → CD13 and CD33 commonly expressed in B-ALL.

●      B cell antigens → PAX5 and CD19 can be positive in → AML with t(8;21)

●      Combination of CD13, CD33 and CD25 is classic for → B-ALL with BCR-ABL1/t(9;22)

●      B cell antigen CD79a common in → T-ALL

Q. What are the 9 recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities that occur in B-cell ALL?

  1. Hyperdiploidy (>50)
  2. Hypodiploidy (24-43)
  3. t(v;11q23);KMT2A-rearranged
  4. t(12;21);ETV6::RUNX1
  5. t(5;14);IGH::IL3
  6. t(1;19);TCF3::PBX1
  7. t(9;22);BCR::ABL1
  8. BCR::ABL1-like
  9. iAMP21 (5+ copies of RUNX1)

WHO2022

 

High hyperdiploidy

51-65 chromosomes

Hypodiploidy

Near-haploid B-ALL/LBL with hypodiploidy (24–31 chromosomes); low-hypodiploid B-ALL/LBL with hypodiploidy (32–39 chromosomes); high-hypodiploid B-ALL/LBL with hypodiploidy (40–43 chromosomes)

iAMP21

B-ALL with iAMP21 B-ALL occurs in ~ 2% of children with ALL, especially older children with median age of 9 years and low WBC counts

BCR::ABL1 fusion

B-ALL with t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)/BCR::ABL1 is seen in ~ 25% of adult patients but only 2-5% in childhood B-ALL

BCR::ABL1 like

B-ALL BCR::ABL1-like share gene expression and phenotypic similarities with B-ALL with BCR::ABL1 fusion and shows significant benefit from targeted therapies

KMT2A rearrangement

B-ALL with KMT2A rearrangement is most common in infants, who often present with very high WBC count and higher rate of CNS involvement

ETV::RUNX1 fusion

B-ALL with t(12;21)(p13.2;q22.1)/ETV6::RUNX1 is common in children, accounting for ~ 25% of B-ALL but rare in infants or adults

ETV::RUNX1 like

 

TCF3::PBX1 fusion

 

IGH::IL3 fusion

B-ALL with t(5;14)(q31.1;q32.3)/IL3::IGH is often accompanied by eosinophilia

TCF3::HLF fusion

B-ALL with HLF rearrangement: TCF3::HLF fusion is characterized by particularly aggressive behavior

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with t(9;22)?

 

Accounts for 25% of adult B-ALL, but only 2-4% of pediatric.

●      Typically CD10, CD19, TdT+ and CD25+ in adults.

●      CD13 and CD33 expression are common.

●      Most pediatric cases produce p190 fusion protein.

●      Adults 50% p210 and 50% p190 fusion protein.

●      Poor prognosis

●      Note: CD25 = Interleukin-2 (IL-2) receptor (alpha chain)

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with t(v;11q23); KMT2A-rearranged?

●      Most common in infants <1 yo

●      Typically present with very high white count (>100)

●      CNS involvement common

●      Often CD10 negative

●      Poor prognosis

Q. What are the most common gene mutations with 11q23 in ALL

●      AF4 on chromosome 4q21 in majority of cases

●      ENL gene on chromosome 19p13

●      AF9 on chromosome 9p22 are common in remaining cases

 

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with t(12;21); ETV6::RUNX1?

●      Also called TEL-AML1 (RUNX1 = AML1)

●      Most common of children B-ALL, 25% of childhood B-ALL cases

●      Characteristic immunophenotype: expression of CD34, near or complete absence of CD9, CD20, and CD66c are relatively specific

●      CD13 CD33 expression is common

●      Very favorable prognosis

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with Hyperdiploidy[QZ8] ? How do you define hyperdiploid?

●      Defined as >50 chromosomes, but usually < 66

●      25-35% of childhood B-ALL

●      7-8% of adult cases

●      Blasts typically CD10+, CD34+, CD45 negative

●      Very favourable prognosis

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with Hypodiploidy - what are the 4 subtypes?

●      Rare <1%

●      Four subtypes:

○      Near-haploid (24-29 chromosomes) (Note: 20’s)

○      Low hypodiploid (33-39 chromosomes) (Note: 30’s)

○      High hypodiploid (40-43 chromosomes) (Note: 40’s)

○      Near-diploid (44-45) (almost normal!)

●      50% low-hypodiploid B-ALL/LBL have a germline TP53 mutation (Li-Fraumeni syndrome AD)

●      Both near-haploid and low/high-hypodiploid have worst prognosis.

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with t(5;14);IGH::IL3?

●      Rare disease <1% of cases in children and adults

●      Translocation juxtaposes IL-3 gene against IGH@ → upregulation of IL-3 that stimulates eosinophilia.

●      Can present with asymptomatic eosinophilia and low/absent blasts in the peripheral blood, or clinical manifestations of hypereosinophilic syndrome with organomegaly, dyspnea, skin involvement, neurological symptoms, thrombo-embolic events, and eosinophilic cardiomyopathy

●      Blasts are CD10+

●      The presence of even small number of blasts and this finding is highly suggestive of this diagnosis.

●      Can be identified on conventional karyotype

●      Prognosis is uncertain; too rare to determine

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with t(1;19);TCF3::PBX1?

●      5% of pediatric cases

●      CD19, CD10, and cytoplasmic mu heavy chain positive.

●      Also show strong expression of CD9 and lack CD34

●      Intermediate

●      Mnemonic to remember the gene names: “The Commonly Forgotten (3) - Peanut Butter Xandwich (1)”

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with BCR::ABL1-like GEP?

●      Lymphoblasts show a pattern of gene expression similar to those in BCR-ABL1 → but lack the translocation.

●      Nothing unique to help identify them → presently no practical way to identify them and no specific morphological or immunophenotypic features to suggest referral for specialized testing

●      Poor prognosis

Q. What are the classic associations and features of B-ALL with iAMP21 - what gene is amplified?

●      Identified by using FISH probes for RUNX1 and defined as → >/= 5 copies of RUNX1 [QZ9] in total or >/= 3 on a single chromosome.

●      Incidence isn’t known in adult populations.

●      Poor prognosis originally, but when treated with aggressive therapy may not be poor prognosis.

Q. What are 5 adverse prognostics features for adult ALL (both B and T-ALL)?

●      Age >60

●      Leukocytes >100

●      Early T-cell precursor immunophenotype [QZ10] (ETP)

●      Genotype: BCR-ABL1; KMT2A (MLL)-AF4, Hypodiploidy <44

●      Positive MRD after induction >0.01%

 

The opposite of these 5 would = 5 favourable prognostics features for adult ALL

 

Q. What are 5 favorable prognostics features for pediatric ALL?

●      Age (1-9)

●      Leukocyte count (<50)

●      Immunophenotype (B-lymphoblastic)

●      Genotype (hyperdiploidy >50, ETV6-RUNX1)

●      Negative minimal residual disease after induction <0.01%

The opposite of these 5 would = 5 adverse prognostics features for pediatric ALL

 

●      Age <1 or >9

●      Leukocyte count (>50)

●      Immunophenotype (T-lymphoblastic)

●      Genotype (anything NOT hyperdiploidy [> 50 chromosomes] or ETV6::RUNX1)

●      Positive MRD after induction (>0.01%)

Cytogenetic abnormalities as prognostic predicators

·       Favorable

o   B-ALL hyperdiploid

o   B-ALL with t(12;21)(p13.2;q22.1)/ETV6::RUNX1

·       Unfavorable

o   B-ALL low hypodiploid

o   B-ALL near haploid

o   B-ALL with t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)/BCR::ABL1

o   B-ALL, BCR::ABL1-like

o   B-ALL with t(v;11q23.3)/KMT2A rearranged, t(4;11)/KMT2A::AFF1 fusion

o   B-ALL with iAMP21

o   B-ALL with TCF3::HLF fusion

o   Complex abnormalities

·       Intermediate

o   B-ALL with t(5;14)(q31.1;q32.3)/IL3::IGH

o   B-ALL with t(1;19)(q23.3;p13.3)/TCF3::PBX1

o   Normal karyotype

o   Any other abnormalities not in favorable or unfavorable categories

Hematogones

 

Q. What is the hematogone maturation pattern and how can you distinguish this from B-cell ALL?

●      Hematogones can be very high and in excess of 20% in relatively normal bone marrows.

●      Hematogones can be morphologically and immunophenotypically indistinguishable from lymphoblasts → always consider them in your DDx for B-ALL

●      Variety of conditions are associated with increased hematogones (see Foucar table below)

●      The most important consideration is the patients age → high percentages of hematogones are much more common with younger ages.

●      Hematogones >25% are not reported in normal or reactive marrows → but below this threshold caution must be exercised as they can be morphologically and immunophenotypically indistinguishable from lymphocytes.

●      Hematogones usually show an → immunophenotypic maturation spectrum → which can enable differentiation from B-cell ALL

●      Figure 1. Comparison of the morphology of hematogones (L) and neoplastic lymphoblasts (R) in bone marrow smears.

○      (A) Several hematogones are illustrated in this bone marrow smear from a 3-year-old boy with immune thrombocytopenia. They bear close resemblance to the neoplastic lymphoblasts illustrated in panel B.

○      (B) Numerous lymphoblasts are present in this bone marrow smear from a 5-year-old girl with precursor B-ALL.

●      Figure 2. Normal maturational sequence of bone marrow B-cell precursors (hematogones). 4 stages of Hematogones are illustrated

●      IP Patterns

○      CD10, 38, 19 & 22 are common to all stages, with variable intensity across stages

○      TdT and CD34 are lost after 1st stage

○      CD10 decreases as CD20 is gained

○      CD45 expression would also increase with maturation

●      # TdT and sIg were not used for assessment of hematogones in this study.

●      * The appearance of sIg is variable among individual cells in different cases, occurring from shortly before to shortly after acquisition of a high level of CD20 expression.

●      Figure 3. Flow cytometry histograms of a BM specimen with increased hematogones.

●      The histograms illustrate the → normal pattern of maturation of B-lymphocyte precursors (hematogones) with the 4-color antibody combination of CD10, CD20, CD22, and CD34.

●      Violet → early-stage hematogones

●      Green → intermediate and late-stage hematogones

●      Blue → mature B cells

 

●      CD45 expression increases with maturation

●      Hematogones → characteristic “stutter” with multiple maturation groups showing spectrum of expression

●      ALL → would lack the maturation spectrum, all events would reside in one cluster with uniform CD10 expression (see red population in flow below)

●      Hematogone CD10 → spectrum, not uniform, broad range is present

●      Most immature population here is turquoise

●      Most mature population is blue with high 20 & 45 and low 10

 

Dense population of immature B lymphoblasts, all in one spot, no maturation spectrum
