T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma

 

Q. What are the requisite criteria to diagnose T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma?

●      Blast cutoff:

○      No defined blast count.

○      WHO recommends the diagnosis should be “avoided” if under 20% blasts.

●      Lymphoblastic lymphoma is a term used if confined to a mass lesion with minimal involvement of peripheral blood and bone marrow.

●      15% of childhood ALL and 25% of cases of adult ALL.

●      85-90% of lymphoblastic lymphomas.

●      Frequently presents with a mediastinal (thymic) mass

Q. Morphology of T-ALL?

●      Blasts are morphologically indistinguishable from blasts in B-cell ALL.

●      In certain cases T-cell ALL blasts can resemble more mature lymphocytes, and immunophenotyping is required to distinguish them from more mature T-cell lymphomas.

Q. What is the typical T-ALL immunophenotype?

●      TdT and variably CD1a, CD2, CD3 (surface or cytoplasmic), CD4, CD5, CD7, and CD8

●      CD7 and cytoplasmic CD3 are most often positive

●      Only CD3 is considered lineage specific

●      Frequent coexpression of CD4 and CD8 but can express only former/latter or neither

●      T lymphoblasts may also coexpress CD10

○      CD10 expression can also be seen in peripheral T-cell lymphoma, most commonly in angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma

●      Aberrant non-lineage antigen expression

○      CD79a 10% of cases

○      CD13 and CD33 20-30% of cases

○      CD117 occasional – associated with FLT3-activation mutations

 

Q. Molecular findings in T-ALL → what 2 clonal populations are possible?

●      T cells → T-cell receptor is almost always clonal.

●      B cells → 20% show B-cell clonality.

Q. Name 4 T-cell ALL mutations (one is a translocation)?

●      NOTCH 1 mutations

●      HOX11 overexpression and HOX11 L2

●      t(9;9)(NUP214-ABL1 fusion) → can use ABL kinase inhibitors (imatinib/dasatinib)

●      CDKN1/2

Q. Cytogenetic studies in T-ALL may show what gene rearrangements on chromosomes 14 and 7?

●      50-70% show cytogenetic abnormalities

●      CG abnormalities typically involve:

○      alpha or delta TR loci at 14q11.2 or

○      beta or gamma locus at 7p

Prognostic features of T-ALL:

  • Longer survival, complete remission (CR) rate, and CR duration in patients with
    • Age < 40 years
    • Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) level < 2x upper limits of normal
    • Absent or single extranodal site of disease
  • Short survival with failure to achieve CR in patients with
    • Age > 40 years
    • LDH level > 2x upper limits of normal
    • Hemoglobin level < 10 g/dL

 

Q. Differential diagnosis of T-ALL

·       B-ALL

·       Mature T-cell lymphoma

·       Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and FGFR1 rearrangement

·       Indolent T-lymphoblastic proliferation

ETP-ALL

Q. What is “Early Thymic Precursor ALL” (ETP)?

●      Early T-precursor lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma (ETP-ALL) is a neoplasm composed of blasts committed to the T-cell lineage with a unique immunophenotype that includes the expression of stem cell markers and/or myeloid lineage markers.

●      Initially reported to be poor when compared with non-ETP ALL

●      Long-term outcomes of paediatric and adult patients with ETP-ALL were comparable to those of patients with other T-ALLs

 

Q. What is immunophenotype of early T precursor ALL (ETP)?

ETP-ALL

Must meet all five criteria for antigen expression:

1.     CD3 (cytoplasmic+; surface−)

2.     Absent myeloperoxidase (< 10% by flow cytometry, < 3% by cytochemistry)

3.     Absent CD1a and CD8

4.     ≥ 25% of blasts with at least one of the following stem cell or myeloid markers: CD34, KIT (CD117), CD13, CD33, CD65, CD11b, HLA-DR

5.     Dim to negative CD5 (< 75% of blasts positive)

Near–ETP-ALL

Criteria 1–4 met but ≥ 75% blasts are CD5+
  • Diagnosed when case of T-ALL meets all of following
    • cCD3(+)
    • Absence of CD1a and CD8 expression (< 5% of blasts positive)
    • Absent to dim CD5 expression (< 75% of blasts positive)
    • Expression (positive in at least 25% of blasts) of 1 or more of following myeloid- or stem cell-associated markers
      • CD117, CD34, HLA-DR, CD13, CD33, CD11b, CD65
    • MPO(-) (< 3%)

·        Suggested diagnostic criteria for ETP-ALL. Just for reference.

ALL cases must be positive for cytoplasmic CD3 positive and CD7 plus the following:

Mandatory criteria (All of the criteria must be present):

1. CD1a negative

2. CD8 negative

3. Surface CD3 negative

4. TCR alpha/beta and TCR gamma/delta negative

5. CD5 negative or dim (<75% of blasts positive)

6. One or more stem cell/myeloid antigens as stated in WHO classification (CD34, HLA-DR, CD13, CD33, CD117, CD11b, and CD65)

Positivity of these markers do not exclude the diagnosis of ETP-ALL

CD2, CD4, CD10

 

Q. What is the role of myeloid mutations in ETP-ALL - name 3 myeloid mutations that may be seen in ETP?

●      Myeloid-associated gene mutations → such as FLT3, NRAS/KRAS, DNMT3A, IDH1, and IDH2, are reported at high frequency in ETP-ALL, while more typical T-ALL-associated mutations such as activating mutations in NOTCH1 or mutations in CDKN1/2 are infrequent

 

Q. What is the entity known as “Indolent T-lymphoblastic Proliferation”?

●      Main differential to consider for T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma.

●      Histologic examination of involved lymph nodes shows infiltration and sometimes replacement by proliferations of lymphoblasts that are less cytologically atypical than the usual T-lymphoblastic lymphoma.

●      Although the blasts have an immature thymic phenotype that can be demonstrated by TdT staining in lymph nodes → the phenotype reflects a developmentally normal, non-aberrant phenotype and the proliferations are NOT clonal

 

Q. What is “Near ETP ALL”?

·       Similar phenotypic profile but CD5 expression in >75% of blasts

Normal Populations Reference:

 

Q. Explain the stages of B cell maturation and differentiation as B cells mature and travel from the BM to the LNs?

(REFERENCE ONLY)

●      Red bar in nucleus indicates → heavy chain gene rearrangement

●      Blue bar indicates → light chain gene rearrangement

●      Black boxes indicate → somatic  hypermutation.

●      Cells coloured in yellow have not encountered antigen, as opposed to antigen-dependent stages shown in violet.

Stages of B Cell Development

The development of B cells is divided into two phases:

1. Bone Marrow (Antigen-Independent Stages)

  • Pro-B Cell:
    • Description: Derived from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). This is the earliest stage of B cell development, focusing on rearranging the heavy chain immunoglobulin (IgH) genes.
    • Markers:
      • CD34: Marker for early progenitor cells.
      • TdT: Enzyme for junctional diversity during V(D)J recombination.
      • CD10, LMO2, CD19, CD79A, and PAX5.
    • Checkpoint: Successful rearrangement of IgH (DJ, then V-DJ) to proceed to the Pre-B stage.
  • Pre-B Cell:
    • Description: Cells express a pre-BCR consisting of a successfully rearranged heavy chain and a surrogate light chain. Light chain rearrangement (V-J) begins at this stage.
    • Markers:
      • CD19, CD79A, PAX5: Continue to be expressed.
    • Checkpoint: Functional pre-BCR signaling allows transition to the immature B cell stage.
  • Immature B Cell:
    • Description: Cells express a complete B cell receptor (BCR) with heavy and light chains (IgM). Negative selection removes self-reactive cells through clonal deletion or receptor editing.
    • Markers:
      • CD19, CD79A, PAX5, and initial CD20 expression.
    • Checkpoint: Non-self-reactive immature B cells migrate to the spleen.

2. Peripheral Lymphoid Tissues (Antigen-Dependent Stages)

  • Transitional B Cell (Spleen):
    • Description: Immature B cells enter the spleen as transitional B cells (T1 and T2) to undergo further selection and maturation.
    • Markers: Express both IgM and low levels of IgD.
  • Mature Naïve B Cell:
    • Description: These cells express fully functional IgM and IgD on their surface. They recirculate between blood, lymph, and secondary lymphoid organs, searching for antigens.
    • Markers:
      • CD19, CD79A, PAX5, CD20, and CD23.
    • Role: Ready to be activated upon antigen encounter.
  • Germinal Center B Cell (After Antigen Encounter in Lymph Nodes):
    • Description: Naïve B cells are activated by antigens, proliferate, and migrate into germinal centers in lymph nodes.
    • Processes:
      • Clonal expansion: Proliferation of antigen-specific B cells.
      • Somatic hypermutation (SHM): Enhances antigen-binding affinity of BCRs.
      • Class-switch recombination (CSR): Switching from IgM/IgD to IgG, IgA, or IgE.
    • Markers:
      • CD38, BCL6, and HGAL.
    • Checkpoint: Selection of high-affinity clones by follicular dendritic cells (FDCs).
  • Memory B Cell:
    • Description: Long-lived cells that ensure rapid responses upon re-exposure to the antigen.
    • Markers: IRF4/MUM1.
    • Role: Reside in secondary lymphoid organs or circulation.
  • Plasma Cell:
    • Description: Terminally differentiated B cells specialized for antibody secretion.
    • Markers:
      • CD38 (re-expressed), BLIMP1, XBP1, and CD138.
    • Role: Produce large amounts of high-affinity antibodies and migrate to bone marrow or peripheral tissues.

Q. What are the stages of normal B-cell differentiation and their relationship to major B-cell neoplasms - List the B cell maturation stage that correlates with the following malignancies - B-ALL, CLL, MCL, MZL, Burkitt, DLBCL, PCM?

 

 

●      B-cell neoplasms correspond to various stages of normal B-cell maturation, although the

●      normal cell counterparts are unknown in some instances.

○      Precursor B cells → which mature in the bone marrow, may undergo apoptosis or develop into → mature naive B cells

○      Mature naive B cells → following exposure to antigen (AG) and blast transformation, may develop into short-lived plasma cells or enter the germinal centre (GC)

■      The GC is where somatic hypermutation and heavy chain class switching occur.

○      GC cells → Centroblasts = the transformed cells of the GC

○      Centroblasts either undergo apoptosis or develop into → centrocytes.

○      Post-GC cells → include both long-lived plasma cells and memory/marginal-zone B cells.

○      Most B cells are activated within the GC, but T-cell-independent activation can take place outside the GC and probably also leads to memory-type B cells.

○      Monocytoid B cells, many of which lack somatic hypermutation, are not illustrated.

●      The red bars → indicate IGH gene rearrangement

●      The blue bars → indicate IG light chain gene rearrangement

●      The black insertions → in red and blue bars indicate somatic hypermutation which occurs in the GC and all subsequently derived cells harbour somatic mutations of their IGH and IG LC genes

 

 

Q. What are the immunophenotypes of T-cell development stages? (Reference Only)

●      1) Lymphoid stem cell (CD34, TdT)

●      2) Early thymocyte (TdT, CD7, cCD3, +/-2 and 5, double negative for CD4 and 8 )

●      3) Cortical thymocyte (TdT, CD7, cCD3, double positive for CD4 and 8, 2, 5, CD1a)

●      4) Medullary thymocyte (TdT, CD4 or 8, CD3, 2, 5, 7)

●      5) Blood T-lymphocyte (CD4 or 8, 2, 5, 7, CD3)

●      Figure 1. T-cell differentiation.

●      T cells mature in the thymus gland and then leave to occupy peripheral lymphoid
tissues.

●      T-cell receptor (TR) genes are shown schematically with a solid red bar indicating absence of rearrangement.

●      The black boxes in the red bars reflect the rearrangements of the TR genes. The double red lines on the cell membrane represent the expressed T-cell receptor complex.

●      Antigen dependent maturation leads to the different T-cell

●      subsets, also illustrated in Fig. 11.05. The phenotypes of several key T-cell subsets are illustrated: T follicular helper (TFH), T regulatory (T-reg),T helper 1(Th1), T helper 2 (Th2), and T helper 17 (Th17)

 

●      Figure 2. T-cell differentiation.

●      T-cell neoplasms correspond to various stages of normal T-cell maturation.

●      Mature T cells include alpha beta and gamma delta T cells, both of which mature in the thymus gland.

●      Recently recognized T-cell subsets include the various types of CD4+ effector T cells, including → T helper 1(Th1),T helper 2(Th2), T regulatory (Treg), T helper 17 (Th17), and T follicular helper (TFH) cells.

Q. In ICC, AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities is defined by presence of 10% blasts. What are the exceptions?

·       AML with BCR::ABL1 has ≥ 20% blast percentage requirement

Q. What AML subtypes in ICC require ≥ 20% blasts?

·       AML with t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2)/BCR::ABL1

·       AML with mutated TP53 (ICC entity only)

·       AML, myelodysplasia-related gene mutations (MRG) (ICC designation only)

·       AML, myelodysplasia-related cytogenetic abnormalities (MRC) (ICC designation only)

·       AML, not otherwise specified (NOS)

Q. Does ICC recognize "Therapy-related" and "germline disorder-associated" as AML entities?

·       No
